newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: FOCUS-S.Africa to shut down phone call-back firms.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-S.Africa to shut down phone call-back firms.

text.p: South Africa's independent telecommunications regulator on Tuesday gave operators two weeks to shut down their 216 million rand a year ($46 million) telephone call-back system or face fines of up to 500,000 rand.

In the first major ruling by the six-member South African Telecommunications Regulatory Authority (Satra), chairman Nape Maepe told a news conference call-back operations were cutting into the profits of the country's Telkom telephone monopoly.

"Satra hereby rules that all callback operations, including their associated support activities, constitute an offence... Operators and customers are hereby duly warned to cease and desist from such unlawful activities," Maepa said.
Call-back operators offer a mechanism to take advantage of cheaper foreign rates by calling a client back after an initial contact and linking them to networks outside South Africa.
"Call backs erode the revenue creation of the international telephone service and the infrastructure, too," said Satra commissioner Tsidi Seane.

Maepe said call-back systems were illegal under South Africa's 1996 Telecommunications Act, which cleared the way for the state-owned Telkom to sell a 30 percent stake to a consortium of U.S. regional Bell SBC Communications Corp and Telekom Malaysia.
He said they also undermined Telkom's ability to extend telephone services to the black majority disadvantaged by 45 years of apartheid.
Maepe gave operators two weeks to close, adding: "We would not make a ruling of this nature if we could not enforce it."
Gianfranco Cicogna, chairman of the South African Callback Association, said the industry was billing about 18 million rand a month and currently was dominated by 10 operators.
"We are shocked that in the South Africa of today, where everybody is consulted about everything, we were not even given a chance to make a presentation before this decision was made," he said.
Cicogna said call-back operations enhanced the international competitiveness of South African business without harming the revenue base of the domestic service provider.
"Our business is growing, but our share of international telephone traffic is staying roughly static at less than six percent," he said.
A Telkom spokesman contested Cicogna's view, however, telling Reuters: "We see our international traffic sliding all the time and we can't afford it."
He said international traffic accounted for about 10 percent of telephone activity and about 80 percent of revenue.
